assignment.title: Practical Assignment — From Raw Footage to Final Edit
assignment.description:
It's time to put everything you've learned in Module 1 into practice.

For this assignment, you will be given a muted basketball video on YouTube. The footage contains no sound, which means you will be responsible for creating the audio experience of your final edit.

Your task is to take the raw footage, bring it into CapCut Mobile, and transform it into a completely new 30-60 second portrait video.

You are not simply cutting the video down. You are expected to think like an editor.

You will select the strongest moments, make multiple cuts, rearrange the footage, reframe the video, add appropriate music, use text where necessary, and create your own interpretation of the footage.

There is no single correct edit. Your creativity and editing decisions are part of the assignment.
assignment.instructions:
STEP 1 - GET THE RAW FOOTAGE

The raw footage for this assignment is a basketball video hosted on YouTube:
https://youtu.be/xee27Eiytes

Visit the link and use the provided video as the raw footage for your assignment.

IMPORTANT - DOWNLOADING THE VIDEO

You were not taught how to download YouTube videos during the lessons, and this was intentional. This is part of the learning experience.

At UCA, you are not expected to figure everything out alone. Your first step is to go to your Peer Buddy Group and discuss with your team members how you can download the video to your mobile device so that you can use it in CapCut.

If you don't know how to download it, ask your Peer Buddy Group for help. You can also go to the Lobby / General Group and ask the wider UCA community for assistance.

This is intentional because one of the things you are learning at UCA is how to ask for help, collaborate, share knowledge, and solve problems together.

STEP 2 - CREATE A 30-60 SECOND VIDEO

Your final video must be between 30 and 60 seconds.

You are free to decide what story, feeling, or experience you want your edit to communicate. You have the same raw footage as everyone else. What you create from that footage is up to you.

STEP 3 - CHANGE THE VIDEO TO PORTRAIT

The original basketball footage is in landscape orientation. Your final video must be in portrait orientation.

Use the aspect-ratio skills you learned in Tuesday's lesson to change your project to a portrait format.

IMPORTANT: Do NOT use a blurred background to fill the empty space. Instead, you must zoom the original footage until it fills the portrait frame.

Because the original footage is landscape, zooming it into a portrait frame will cause some parts of the original image to be cropped out. This is intentional. Your job is to decide what should remain visible.

STEP 4 - REFRAME YOUR FOOTAGE

When you zoom the footage to fill the portrait frame, you will need to position it carefully. Think about the most important subject in each shot. For example:

- If the player has the ball, make sure the player remains visible.
- If the ball is moving toward a particular area, position the frame so the movement can still be followed.
- If the player's face is important to the moment, you may choose to frame the face.
- If the ball movement is the most interesting part, you may choose to focus on the ball.

You don't have to keep the same framing throughout the entire video. Use the frame creatively.

STEP 5 - MAKE MULTIPLE CUTS

You are encouraged to make multiple cuts throughout the footage. Do not simply take one 30-60 second section and place it into the timeline.

Break the footage into different sections and experiment with how they work together. For example, your edit could include a shot showing the full player, a tighter shot focusing on the player's movement, a shot focusing on the ball, a shot showing the player's face, and another shot showing the action from a different moment.

You can cut between these moments to create your own rhythm and visual experience. There is no required number of cuts. Be creative.

STEP 6 - REARRANGE THE FOOTAGE

This is a major part of the assignment. Do not simply allow the video to play in its original sequence.

Select different moments from the footage and rearrange them to create a new sequence. You can move moments earlier, move moments later, combine different sections, repeat a useful moment if it improves the edit, cut between different actions, and create your own visual progression.

Your final video should feel like your edit, not simply a shortened version of the original video.

Remember: you are not just cutting footage. You are constructing an experience.

STEP 7 - ADD MUSIC / AUDIO

The original footage has no sound. You are therefore responsible for choosing the audio for your final video.

Find music that fits the basketball footage and the type of edit you are creating. Think about energy, mood, pace, rhythm, timing, and the feeling you want the viewer to experience.

Your music should complement the footage. Don't choose a song simply because you like it. Ask yourself: does this music make sense for this video?

Your audio choice will be part of your grade.

STEP 8 - USE TEXT

You are required to demonstrate your ability to use basic text. Use text where it adds value to your video.

Your text could introduce the video, communicate an idea, add context, emphasize a moment, tell part of the story, or create a particular mood.

Pay attention to position, alignment, timing, size, readability, and placement within the frame. Don't place text randomly. Think about where the viewer's attention is and make sure your text is positioned appropriately.

Your use of text and its placement will be graded.

STEP 9 - EXPORT YOUR VIDEO

When your edit is complete, export the final video from CapCut using the following required settings:

Resolution: 1080p
Frame Rate: 30 FPS

Make sure your final exported video is between 30-60 seconds, is in portrait orientation, has no blurred background, is properly framed, plays correctly, and uses the required export settings.

YOUR FINAL SUBMISSION

Once you have completed your edit:

1. Export your video from CapCut.
2. Confirm that it meets the requirements.
3. Upload your export to Google Drive, YouTube or Dropbox and set it to "anyone with the link".
4. Submit the link here on the Assignment Portal.

Video files are too large to upload directly, so you submit a link to your finished video.
assignment.requirements:
WHAT YOU WILL BE GRADED ON

Your final video will be assessed based on how well you apply the skills taught throughout Monday and Tuesday.

1. CUTTING - Are your cuts clean and intentional? Are unnecessary sections removed?
2. CLIP ARRANGEMENT - Did you creatively rearrange the footage? Did you avoid simply following the original sequence?
3. PORTRAIT FRAMING - Did you correctly convert the landscape footage into portrait? Did you zoom the footage to fill the frame? No blurred background. Did you position the frame intelligently so that important subjects remain visible?
4. STORYTELLING - Does your final edit communicate something? Do your clips work together to create a coherent experience?
5. MUSIC / AUDIO - Does your chosen music fit the basketball footage? Does the music complement the pacing and mood of the edit?
6. TEXT - Did you use text effectively? Is it properly positioned, aligned, timed, and readable? Does it contribute to the video rather than simply being added because it is required?
7. CREATIVITY - Did you make creative decisions with the footage? Did you experiment with different cuts, framing, sequencing, and moments?
8. EXPORT SETTINGS - Did you export the final video correctly? Required settings: 1080p - 30 FPS.

FINAL CHECKLIST

[ ] My video is between 30-60 seconds
[ ] I used the provided basketball footage
[ ] I changed the video from landscape to portrait
[ ] I zoomed the footage to fill the portrait frame
[ ] I did not use a blurred background
[ ] Important subjects remain visible
[ ] I made multiple intentional cuts
[ ] I removed unnecessary footage
[ ] I rearranged the original sequence
[ ] My clips form a logical sequence
[ ] I added appropriate music/audio
[ ] I used text appropriately
[ ] My text is properly positioned and aligned
[ ] I exported at 1080p
[ ] I exported at 30 FPS
[ ] I uploaded the final exported video and submitted the link

THE CHALLENGE

Remember, everyone is starting with the same footage. Your advantage is not having different footage. Your advantage is how you see it.

One person might focus on the player's movement. Another might focus on the ball. Another might create an energetic sports montage. Another might tell a completely different story through their text and sequencing.

There is no single correct creative direction. What matters is whether your final video demonstrates the skills you have been taught and whether your editing decisions are intentional, clean, creative, and effective.

Take the raw footage. Make it yours.
